newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says it wants to defuse crisis with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iraq says it wants to defuse crisis with U.S..

text.p: Iraq said on Saturday it hoped its decision to suspend missile attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes enforcing no-fly zones would help defuse the military standoff with Washington.

"Iraq, by suspending its military reaction to violations of our national airspace, until further notice, provides another proof of its strong keenness to avoid the eruption of crises," the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya said in a front-page editorial.
The newspaper reiterated that Iraq's ceasefire was temporary and meant to "strip America of excuses and pretexts to commit a new crime".

But with the continued military build-up in the region by the United States, President Saddam Hussein held talks with senior military aides about the deployment of Iraq's surface-to-air missile forces and how to confront any attack.

"The meeting discussed...the improvement of confrontation means in the face of any evil possibility that would be necessitated by the future if Almighty wants that, or Satan pushes the enemy into his vicious abysses," the official Iraqi News Agency INA reported.
The U.S. decision to dispatch warships, aircraft carriers and bombers close to Iraq illustrated that Washington was applying "a cowboy method" in dealing with events, Jumhouriya paper said.
In a surprise move, Iraq backed down on Friday on a pledge to shoot at Western planes patrolling its airspace.
Baghdad's announcement came just hours after U.S. Stealth bombers arrived in Kuwait as part of a U.S. military buildup in the Gulf that also includes the dispatch of 5,000 more troops.
Iraq's decision, issued by the ruling Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) chaired by President Saddam Hussein, went into effect at midnight Friday (2000 GMT).
The first U.S. reaction was cautious, with officials saying they would look at actions not statements.

Iraqi newspaper headlines said Iraq's suspension of attacks on U.S. aircraft -- this week Iraq fired missiles, but missed, at aircraft patrolling no-fly zones in the country's north and south -- was made in response to an initiative from Russia.

Anti-U.S. remarks and commentaries filled the inside pages. The official al-Qadissiya said U.S. theats to use force against Iraq "led to further isolation for America, aggravating its international crisis and flung it into moral collapse and political bankruptcy."

The Iraqi information minister, Abdul-al-Ghani Abd-al-Ghafur, separately lambasted the U.S. state department spokesman Nicholas Burns for accusing Saddam of squandering money on palaces and stowing some in foreign bank accounts.
"They are the palaces of the Iraqi people that they have built for Saddam Hussein...," Ghafur said in a statement reported by the Iraqi News Agency.
Ghafur also denied that Saddam had any secret accounts and suggested that if the bank accounts existed the United States should confiscate the money.
"I say to them (Americans), take all the money registered in the name of Saddam Hussein in foreign banks."

A poem ridiculed Madeleine Albright, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, saying her smiles hid the "bitter humiliation" her country suffered with the collapse of its plans in northern Iraq, under the protection of a U.S.-led allied force since the end of the 1991 Gulf War.
Iraqi troops two weeks ago went into the region to provide military assistance to Kurdish rebels of Massoud Barzani, helping them oust rivals from most of Iraqi Kurdistan.
The incursion into northern Iraq prompted U.S. 44 cruise missile strikes on what the United States called military targets in southern Iraq last week.
Washington also widened a no-fly zone over southern Iraq from Iraq's border with Kuwait northwards to the outskirts of Baghdad.
